stem: Which clinical scenario best fits an acquired paediatric heart disease rather than a congenital lesion?

options.text: A school-aged child develops cardiac inflammation 3 weeks after Group A streptococcal pharyngitis
A newborn with a duct-dependent circulation needs prostaglandin E1 to maintain the ductus arteriosus
A baby develops a ventricular septal defect murmur only after pulmonary vascular resistance falls
A normal newborn is reviewed again at 6 weeks because coarctation can be missed initially
A neonate has right ventricular dominance that gradually diminishes through childhood

explanation: Acute rheumatic fever is the correct answer because it is an acquired inflammatory heart disease that can occur 10 days to 6 weeks after Group A streptococcal pharyngitis.

rationale: Acute rheumatic fever is an acquired disease after Group A streptococcal infection, whereas the other options describe congenital or normal transitional cardiovascular findings.

optionExplanations.A: Correct because cardiac inflammation appearing 3 weeks after Group A streptococcal pharyngitis fits acute rheumatic fever, an acquired paediatric heart disease.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because prostaglandin E1 use for a duct-dependent circulation describes a congenital cardiac lesion.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because a ventricular septal defect is a congenital lesion that becomes more apparent after pulmonary vascular resistance falls.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because delayed review for coarctation reflects a congenital lesion that may be missed on the newborn examination.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because right ventricular dominance in the newborn is a normal transitional pattern, not acquired disease.
